prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms enables frequency standards at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a compact, original idea with a precisely identifiable origin: Katori's proposal that atoms confined in a lattice at a magic wavelength can be probed without Doppler, recoil or net light-shift error, followed by Ye's group taking strontium lattice clocks to roughly 1e-18 systematic uncertainty and stability. The consequences are concrete and already measured: clock-to-clock comparisons across laboratories, tests of the constancy of fundamental constants, centimetre-scale relativistic geodesy, and a leading role in the coming redefinition of the second. The attribution is the cleanest on our shortlist, a two-person share that matches the supplied credit without forcing us to leave out an obvious originator. Maturity is high, with several independent groups reproducing and surpassing the performance. As a theorist of atomic structure and precision spectroscopy I can judge the physics directly: the magic-wavelength condition is a statement about differential polarisabilities, which is exactly the kind of atomic-structure calculation that decides whether such a clock can work at all.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize covered quantum control of single trapped ions, which was the basis of the first ion clocks, so a sceptic can call lattice clocks an excellent refinement of established metrology rather than a new discovery. A second concern is that the practical payoff, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened, and ion-clock groups (not on the credited list) might argue that they share priority for the 1e-18 regime. Finally, B006 has broader opening support in this committee than any other entry, and I should not let a field-proximity preference override that signal.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks topological insulators first, with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan as a theory-plus-two-experiments trio, while acknowledging that leaving out Mele and the HgTe proposers is a real fairness problem.
responses.response: I agree that B006 is scientifically deep and mature, and I ranked it third, not low. But the attribution problem you name is exactly my hesitation. Colleagues propose three different trios (with Hasan, or with Mele), and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe realisation. A prize that excludes one of Kane and Mele, or excludes the 3D discovery, would be contested in a way a two-person clock prize is not. Strength of opening support is not the same as an attribution we can defend, so I would keep B006 as my first alternative and not my preferred prize unless we can agree on a defensible split.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first, calling it the most compelling case from an atomic-physics and measurement viewpoint, but concedes that the novelty relative to the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize has to be argued.
responses.response: We agree on the ranking, but we are both atomic physicists, and I want to be careful that this shared background is not doing the work of an argument. The distinctness case rests on the physics. The comb provided the optical-frequency counting tool, Wineland's work provided single-ion control, and neither provided a way to interrogate a large ensemble of neutral atoms free of motional and light-shift errors. That is Katori's contribution and it is what yields the statistical advantage Ye exploited. I think that is enough to make the clock a separate invention, but I accept that the committee must decide whether it clears the bar and I do not regard the point as settled.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, as a case where a band-structure prediction led directly to a new experimental field of correlated and superconducting phases.
responses.response: The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 observations is an elegant theory-experiment pair and the attribution is clean, which I give real weight. My reservation is maturity: you yourself note that the pairing mechanism is unresolved, and several of us (Johansson, Mehlig, Pearce) call the timing somewhat early. A prize would rest on the existence of flat-band-driven phases and not on an explained mechanism. The lattice clock performance is quantified, reproduced and cross-compared, so I put it ahead, though I would not object strongly to B017 in a later year.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, as a clean transfer of strong coupling to circuits that is distinct from the 2025 prize and underlies most superconducting processors, while discounting his own enthusiasm as a worker in the area.
responses.response: I put B038 second and share your view that it is a clean, original transfer of cavity-QED ideas. Where I differ is on timing and credit. Kroll, Eriksson and Pearce all point to the 2025 circuit prize, and Girvin is outside the credited names although he co-authored the 2004 theory proposal, so the theory share is not clean. I would not rule B038 out, but I would not place it first, and I think the committee should avoid two prizes in the same superconducting-circuit community in consecutive years unless the new content is clearly separate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as a distinct invention from the earlier comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) prizes, and how much weight the pending redefinition of the second should carry.
Whether ion-clock pioneers or other lattice-clock proposers should share credit, which the supplied names do not address.
How to weigh the clearly broader opening support for B006 against its unresolved attribution among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan and the HgTe proposers.
My own field proximity to atomic precision spectroscopy may lead me to overrate the clock case.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the shortlisted candidates from the provided profile. My documented collaborations (Anne L'Huillier, the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and others) concern attosecond physics and highly charged ions, and none of the credited names on B047, B006 or B038 appears among them. I note general field proximity to the atomic-physics entries (B047, B031, B034).
